title: Pre-Prohibition Lager Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: What pre-Prohibition lager was, why it used corn or rice, how it differs from modern light lager and how to taste one.
teaser: American lager before 1920 was fuller, more bitter and more interesting than what replaced it. Here is what it tasted like.
standfirst: Before Prohibition, American brewers made a pilsner-style lager that was more flavourful than the light lager that later took over. Brewers have revived it under names like classic American pilsner. Here is the story and the style.
sections:
In the nineteenth century, German immigrants brought lager brewing to the United States. They wanted to make the pale lagers of home, but the local barley was different. American six-row barley had more protein and more husk than the two-row barley of central Europe. Brewed on its own, it gave hazy, harsh beer.

The solution was an adjunct. Brewers added corn or rice to dilute the protein, lighten the body and improve clarity. Six-row barley had plenty of enzymes to convert the extra starch. The resulting beer became the standard American lager of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
What the style looks like on paper

The BJCP describes pre-Prohibition lager at roughly 4.5 to 6% ABV, with bitterness around 25 to 40 IBU and a pale straw to gold colour. Corn or rice typically makes up around 20 to 30% of the grist. Corn gives a slightly sweet, grainy roundness. Rice gives a drier, crisper finish.

That bitterness range is the big surprise for modern drinkers. It is far above today's mass-market American light lager, which sits in single figures to low teens. Pre-Prohibition lager was a properly hopped beer.

Body sits in the middle. The adjunct keeps it lighter than an all-malt German pilsner, yet the higher starting gravity stops it feeling watery. A good example is crisp enough to drink on a hot day and has enough malt to stand up to a plate of food. That balance is what revivalists are chasing when they brew it today.
Hops from both sides of the Atlantic

American brewers of the era often bittered with Cluster, a native American hop variety with a firm, slightly earthy and blackcurrant-like character. For aroma, many imported German or Czech hops such as Saaz and Hallertau. The combination gave a beer with a clean, rustic bitterness and a gentle floral, spicy nose.

Modern revivals often use the same approach. Cluster is still grown. Noble hops are easy to find. Some brewers also experiment with newer American varieties, though purists argue that drifts away from the historical character.

Prohibition shut down legal brewing in the United States from 1920 to 1933. Many breweries closed for good. Those that survived came back into a changed market, with lighter tastes, rationing during the Second World War and a push towards cheaper, milder beer.

Over the following decades American lager grew lighter in body, lower in bitterness and higher in adjunct. The hoppier pre-Prohibition style faded from view. Homebrewers and historians revived it from the 1990s onwards. It now appears on craft beer lists as a reminder that adjunct lager does not have to mean bland lager.
A useful lesson for Indian brewing

Indian brewers use rice and maize every day. Our guide to rice and maize adjuncts in India covers how they are cooked and mashed. Pre-Prohibition lager proves that a 25% adjunct beer can still be full of character if the hops and malt are given room.

The practical detail that matters is the cereal cook. Raw maize grits and broken rice need to be boiled before they join the main mash, because their starch gelatinises at higher temperatures than barley starch. Skip that step and the starch stays locked up, leaving a thin wort and a hazy beer.

Serve it at 4 to 7 °C in a pilsner glass. Look for good clarity and a lasting white head. The aroma should show clean grainy malt, a touch of corn sweetness or rice crispness and a light floral or spicy hop note.

On the palate you want medium body, firm bitterness and a clean, dry finish. A strong cooked corn or cabbage smell points to DMS, a fault often caused by a weak boil or slow cooling. Fruity notes suggest the lager yeast ran too warm. Neither belongs in a well made example.

Freshness matters as much as recipe. Like any pale lager, this style loses its hop aroma and picks up stale, papery notes when it sits warm. A can that has spent a month in a hot shop will taste flat next to the same beer from a cold tap. Check the packaging date where you can.

Many beer lovers dismiss corn and rice as cheap fillers. Tasting a good pre-Prohibition lager next to a light lager shows the real story: the adjunct shapes the body, while the hops and malt decide whether the beer is interesting. Learning to separate those effects is a core sensory skill.

Start with three glasses: an all-malt pilsner, a pre-Prohibition lager and a mass-market light lager. Taste them in that order. Note body, bitterness and finish. You will learn more about adjuncts in ten minutes than in a dozen arguments online.
faqs: It is the pilsner-style American lager brewed before 1920, made with six-row barley and corn or rice, with more bitterness than modern light lager.
Why did American brewers add corn and rice?
Six-row American barley was high in protein. Corn and rice diluted that protein, lightened the body and improved clarity.
Around 25 to 40 IBU, much more bitter than modern mass-market American light lager.
Is classic American pilsner the same thing?
Yes. Classic American pilsner is another name used for the same revived style.
